concept.body: A chord joins two points ON the circle. In the same circle (or congruent circles), congruent chords cut congruent arcs and congruent central angles — both directions. The engine is triangle congruence on the radii: SSS (chords to angles) or SAS (angles to chords). Special case: the chord of a 60° arc equals the radius.

explanationVariants: The lock copies the measure: congruent chords cut 40° arcs alike.

widget.prompt: Chord PQ cuts a 40° arc; chord RS ≅ PQ in the same circle. Arc of RS = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 20 halves — halving is inscribed-angle business. Congruent chords copy arcs: 40°.

steps.body: A **chord** is a segment with both endpoints on the circle — the diameter is just the chord that happens to pass through the center. Every chord cuts off an arc, and the two are locked together: **congruent chords cut congruent arcs**, and vice versa (in the same circle, or in congruent circles).
Equal chords sit equally far from the centre.

predict.prompt: Two chords in the SAME circle happen to have the same length. Must they sit the same distance from the centre?

options.label: Always — equal chords are always equally far from the centre
Not necessarily — it depends where around the circle each one sits
Only if the two chords are parallel to each other

predict.reveal: Always. Half the chord, the distance to the centre, and the radius form a right triangle — fix the radius and the chord and the distance has no freedom left. Slide the chord and watch the distance readout depend on length alone, never on where it sits.

widget.prompt: Radius 10. Slide the chord until it measures 12.
widget.successFeedback: A chord of 12 sits 8 from the centre — half-chord 6, distance 8, radius 10: the 6-8-10 triangle. Every chord of length 12 in this circle sits at that same distance, which IS the theorem: equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and they cut off equal arcs. Distance and chord length are locked together by r² = d² + (half-chord)².
widget.lowFeedback: The chord is shorter than 12 — it has drifted too far out. Chords shrink as they leave the centre.
widget.highFeedback: The chord is longer than 12 — bring it further from the centre.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate circle measurements while tangent, chord, radius, and power relationships update together.

explanationVariants: Congruent chords cut congruent arcs: the second arc is also 75°.
Same circle + same chord length = same arc: 75°.

widget.prompt: In one circle, chord AB cuts a 75° arc. Chord CD is congruent to AB. What arc does CD cut?

commonErrors.feedback: 150 doubles as if an inscribed angle were involved — the chord-arc lock copies the measure directly: 75°.
37.5 halves — halving belongs to INSCRIBED angles. Congruent chords: equal arcs, 75°.
105 = 180 − 75 supplements — no supplement here, just the SSS lock: 75°.

steps.body: The lock runs through the **central angle**: chord ↔ central angle ↔ arc, each pair matched. A 60° central angle is special: its two radii and the chord form a triangle with two equal sides and 60° between them — equilateral, so **the chord of a 60° arc equals the radius**.

explanationVariants: A 60° central angle makes the radii-chord triangle equilateral: chord = radius = 9.
Isosceles with a 60° apex is equilateral — all sides 9.

widget.prompt: A circle has radius 9. How long is the chord that cuts a 60° arc?

commonErrors.feedback: 18 is the DIAMETER (the 180° chord). The 60° chord closes an equilateral triangle: 9.
4.5 halves the radius — the 60° apex makes all three sides EQUAL: 9.
13.5 = 1.5 × 9 has no triangle behind it — equilateral means chord = radius = 9.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 60° apex between equal radii ⇒ equilateral ⇒ chord = 9.

explanationVariants: Equal arcs pull equal central angles (arcs ARE their central angles), and SAS on the radii then matches the chords.
The lock is two-way: 110° arcs ⇒ congruent chords.

widget.prompt: Two arcs in the same circle both measure 110°. What follows about their chords?

options.label: The chords are congruent — the arc-chord lock runs both directions
options.feedback: Equal arcs give equal central angles, and SAS (radius-angle-radius) matches the chords. Converse secured.

options.label: Nothing — the theorem only runs from chords to arcs
options.feedback: The converse holds too: equal arcs ⇒ equal central angles ⇒ SAS ⇒ equal chords.

options.label: The chords are parallel
options.feedback: Equal arcs say nothing about orientation — the chords could cross. What's guaranteed is equal LENGTH.

options.label: The chords are perpendicular
options.feedback: The theorem promises nothing about the angle between the chords — only their congruence, via the central angles.

widget.prompt: A circle has radius 7. What is the length of the longest possible chord?

commonErrors.feedback: 7 is the radius — the champion chord is the DIAMETER, twice that: 14 (cutting a 180° semicircle).
44 ≈ 2π(7) is the circumference — a path around, not a chord across. The diameter: 14.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The diameter, 2 × 7 = 14, cutting a 180° arc — no chord can exceed it.

hints: Six equal arcs share 360° — how big is each?
Each 60° arc's chord closes an equilateral triangle with the radii.
Six such chords make the perimeter.
explanationVariants: Each arc is 60°, so each chord equals the radius 5 — the inscribed regular hexagon's famous property. Perimeter = 6 × 5 = 30.
Chord-of-60° = radius: six sides of 5 give 30.

widget.prompt: Six points split a circle of radius 5 into six EQUAL arcs, and consecutive points are joined by chords (a regular hexagon). Find the hexagon's perimeter.

commonErrors.feedback: 31.42 ≈ 2π(5) is the CIRCUMFERENCE — the hexagon's straight chords come up short of the curve: 6 × 5 = 30.
25 = 5² squares the radius — each 60° chord EQUALS the radius, and there are six: 30.
60 is each arc's degree measure — the perimeter wants lengths: 6 chords × 5 = 30.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Each 60° chord = r = 5; perimeter = 30 — just under the 31.4 circumference, as straight cuts must be.

takeaways: Congruent chords ↔ congruent central angles ↔ congruent arcs (SSS/SAS on the radii).
The 60° chord equals the radius — equilateral triangle, hexagon shortcut.
The diameter is the longest chord, cutting the 180° semicircle.
steps.teaser: Next: drop a perpendicular from the center and watch it split a chord perfectly.
